title: Focal-onset seizure with Jacksonian march + Todd paralysis: focal structural abnormality
vignette: A 40-year-old man comes to the emergency department 30 minutes after experiencing a seizure. Over the past 3 months, the patient has had several episodes of brief twitching of the right hand, but today the abnormal movement gradually progressed to involve the entire right upper extremity, followed by shaking of the whole body for about a minute. He also lost consciousness and urinated involuntarily during the event. The patient feels groggy and has a mild headache. He has no other medical conditions but reports several concussions from playing football in college. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows mild weakness of right hand grip but is otherwise normal. This patient's seizure presentation is most suggestive of which of the following etiologic processes?

clues.text: several episodes of brief twitching of the right hand
clues.note: Recurrent stereotyped twitching of ONE body part indicates focal-onset seizures localized to a single hemisphere (contralateral motor cortex).

clues.text: gradually progressed to involve the entire right upper extremity
clues.note: A 'Jacksonian march' - spread along the motor homunculus - is characteristic of a FOCAL seizure originating in a discrete cortical region.

clues.text: followed by shaking of the whole body
clues.note: Secondary generalization (focal to bilateral tonic-clonic) with loss of consciousness and incontinence - the focal seizure spread to both hemispheres.
Repetitive head trauma can create a focal structural abnormality (scar/gliosis) that serves as a seizure focus.

clues.text: mild weakness of right hand grip
clues.note: Postictal focal weakness (Todd paralysis) in the region where the seizure began strongly suggests an underlying FOCAL structural lesion.

whatMatters: Focal motor twitching that MARCHES up the limb, then secondarily generalizes, with postictal focal weakness (Todd paralysis) and a history of head trauma = a FOCAL-ONSET seizure. The most common cause of focal seizures is a FOCAL STRUCTURAL brain abnormality. Answer B.
strategy: Localize the seizure: onset in one hand -> march -> secondary generalization, plus postictal focal deficit = focal onset from one hemisphere. Focal-onset seizures most commonly arise from a focal STRUCTURAL lesion (tumor, stroke, scar/gliosis, hippocampal sclerosis). Reject processes that act GLOBALLY and cause generalized-onset seizures without localizing features: diffuse hypoperfusion, neuroexcitatory substances, and metabolic disturbances; genetic epilepsy syndromes usually present in childhood.

eliminations.label: Diffuse hypoperfusion - global, not focal
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: global reduction in cerebral blood flow. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it affects the brain diffusely and would cause generalized symptoms/syncope, not a focal march with postictal focal weakness. ✅ Correct if: global hypoxic-ischemic events (e.g., cardiac arrest, syncope).

eliminations.label: Genetic epilepsy syndrome - usually childhood, generalized
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: inherited epilepsy (e.g., juvenile myoclonic, absence). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: these typically begin in childhood/adolescence and are often generalized without a focal structural lesion or Todd paralysis; onset at 40 with focal march and trauma points elsewhere. ✅ Correct if: childhood-onset generalized epilepsy with normal imaging.

eliminations.label: Neuroexcitatory substance - global effect
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: stimulant/toxin-induced seizures. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: substances act on the brain diffusely, favoring generalized-onset seizures without a fixed focal march or postictal focal deficit. ✅ Correct if: acute intoxication/withdrawal with generalized seizures.

eliminations.label: Neuronal metabolic disturbance - global
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: electrolyte/glucose derangements (hyponatremia, hypoglycemia). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: metabolic causes act globally and produce generalized seizures, not a localized focal onset with Todd paralysis (hyperglycemia can rarely cause focal seizures, but there's no metabolic clue here). ✅ Correct if: seizure with an identified metabolic derangement.

reasoning: Focal hand twitching that marches up the arm = focal-onset seizure from one hemisphere
Secondary generalization + postictal focal weakness (Todd paralysis) confirm a focal origin
History of repetitive head trauma suggests a focal structural lesion (scar/gliosis)
-> focal structural brain abnormality; answer B
mechanism: FOCAL-ONSET seizures arise from a region of hypersynchronized, hyperexcitable neurons in a SINGLE cerebral hemisphere (in contrast to generalized-onset seizures, which begin bilaterally). Symptoms map to the involved cortex: motor cortex involvement causes contralateral twitching/jerking, and spread along the motor homunculus produces a JACKSONIAN MARCH. Focal seizures can secondarily generalize (focal to bilateral tonic-clonic) with loss of consciousness and incontinence, and are frequently followed by a transient POSTICTAL FOCAL NEUROLOGIC DEFICIT (TODD PARALYSIS) in the region of onset. The most common underlying cause of focal-onset seizures is a FOCAL STRUCTURAL brain abnormality - tumor, stroke, cortical malformation, hippocampal sclerosis, or post-traumatic scar/gliosis (relevant given this patient's repeated concussions). Diffuse/global processes (hypoperfusion, toxins, metabolic derangements) and most genetic epilepsy syndromes cause generalized-onset seizures without a localizing focal march or Todd paralysis.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Neuro > seizures: focal (partial) onset in one hemisphere; Jacksonian march; focal to bilateral tonic-clonic; Todd paralysis (postictal focal weakness); most common cause = focal structural lesion (tumor, stroke, sclerosis, trauma).

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Focal march + secondary generalization + Todd paralysis = focal onset -> structural focus.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on focal vs generalized onset, Jacksonian march, Todd paralysis, secondary generalization, or gliosis? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Hypoperfusion, toxins, metabolic disturbance act GLOBALLY (generalized); genetic epilepsy = childhood-onset, usually generalized.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: focal-onset seizure (march + Todd paralysis) -> focal structural abnormality; look for tumor/stroke/scar.

keywords.back: Focal structural abnormality (tumor, stroke, scar, sclerosis)
Seizure spread along the motor homunculus (focal onset)
Transient postictal focal weakness (localizes the focus)
Secondary generalization of a focal seizure
Cortical scar / gliosis as a focus

firstAid.detail: Neuro: single-hemisphere focus; march + Todd paralysis; structural cause.
Neuro > head trauma -> focal scar seizure focus.

memoryHook: A seizure that starts in one hand, marches up the arm, then leaves that hand weak (Todd) is pointing a finger at ONE spot in the brain - a focal structural lesion.
